prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Checkers on an 8x8 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(my_men, my_kings, opp_men, opp_kings, color) -> tuple[tuple[int, int], tuple[int, int]]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `my_men` is a list of squares containing your regular pieces. - `my_kings` is a list of squares containing your kings. - `opp_men` is a list of squares containing opponent regular pieces. - `opp_kings` is a list of squares containing opponent kings. - `color` is your color: `'b'` for black which moves downwards (to lower row values) and `'w'` for white which moves upwards (to higher row values). - Squares use coordinates: row `0`-`7`, column `0`-`7`. - `(0, 0)` is the bottom-left corner; rows increase bottom-to-top and columns increase left-to-right. - Only dark squares are playable. # Action / Return Format - Return a move as a tuple: `((from_row, from_col), (to_row, to_col))`. - `from_row`, `to_row`, `from_col`, `to_col` are coordinates `0..7`. - (`from_row`, `from_col`) has to be a coordinate of a piece that is yours and (`to_row`, `to_col`) has to be the destination square.Return a legal move; captures are mandatory when available. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm considering the checkers rules more carefully—whether kings are flying or short, and how multi-jump captures might be represented in the move API, since the interface only returns a single from/to pair. I need to design the move logic to handle these ambiguities robustly given the standard 8x8 setup with black moving downward and white upward.

Actually, thinking about it more, the lack of any "must continue" state suggests the engine likely treats a full multi-jump sequence as one move from origin to final landing square rather than stepping through intermediate captures. Since I can't be certain, I'll weigh which assumption is safer if wrong and lean toward whichever failure mode seems less costly.

Since the engine description implies a simple implementation, the more likely convention is that the turn stays with the same player after a jump if further captures are available from the new position, rather than expecting the whole multi-jump sequence returned at once. I'll go with returning single-jump segments rather than the full compound move.

I'll go with standard English draughts rules: men move and capture only forward, kings move one step in any direction and capture any direction — sticking with this since it's the most standard interpretation of "Checkers."

For the engine, I'm planning alpha-beta search with iterative deepening under a tight time budget, evaluating material (weighting kings higher than men), piece advancement, back-row defense, and mobility, with captures prioritized in move ordering. I'll represent the board as a flat 64-cell array with simple integer codes for empty squares, men, and kings, normalizing direction based on which side is moving so the same logic works for both players.

I need to handle move generation carefully: men capture only forward while kings can jump in any direction, multi-jump sequences must be generated recursively, and captures should force promotion to end the sequence per standard rules. Since captures are mandatory, I'll extend search depth when forced captures occur, similar to a quiescence search, and check the clock regularly during iterative deepening to stay within time limits.

My evaluation function weighs material heavily (men vs kings), rewards advancement toward the back row, gives small bonuses for center control and keeping the back rank guarded early, and treats having no legal moves as a loss. I'm aiming for roughly depth 6-8 within a fraction of a second using alpha-beta pruning.

Now I'm starting to write the Python implementation, beginning with constants for piece types and the time budget before defining the core move-generation logic.

Writing board setup and move generation...

For multi-jump capture recursion, I'll keep captured pieces on the board but track which ones have been jumped in a set, since jumped pieces block landing squares but can't be captured twice anyway.

Writing capture recursion logic...

Writing apply-move and evaluation functions...

Fleshing out the negamax search itself: quiescence-style cutoffs at depth zero unless a capture forces extension, move ordering favoring promotions and captures, and recursive evaluation with sign flipping between sides. Now I'm weighing how to key the transposition table efficiently, since converting the whole board to a tuple every node could get costly.

I settle on using tuple(board) paired with side as the key since Python tuples hash fast, storing depth, value, flag, and best move per entry to support move ordering across iterations. For the root, I'll use iterative deepening from depth 1 up to 20, keeping the best move found from the last fully completed depth.

If time runs out mid-search, I fall back to the previous depth's result rather than trusting a partial one. I also add a safety net: if anything throws an exception or no result is ready, just return the first legal move available to avoid crashing.

For representing multi-jumps, the pair format for moves strongly suggests a step-based design—after each jump, check the landing square for further jumps and restrict the next choice to those, rather than trying to encode a whole jump sequence at once.

Assuming captured pieces get removed immediately after each jump keeps things tractable, since otherwise my policy might mistakenly try to re-capture the same piece. There's no reliable way to bias my search toward continuing the same piece's capture chain versus switching to another piece's, though I could try keeping module-level state between calls to track the planned sequence if the board state matches expectations.

I'm setting up a persistence mechanism: storing a pending multi-jump path with the expected board state after each step, so if the next call's board matches, I return the next segment of the planned sequence rather than re-searching from scratch. This requires tracking the full path of landing squares in the capture move generation.

For timing, I'm budgeting around 0.55 seconds out of the 1-second limit to leave room for Python overhead and search variance.

Writing move generation logic...

Writing capture recursion logic...

Then I'm writing a helper to apply a move: clearing captured pieces, promoting men that reach the back row, and placing the piece at its destination.

Now I'm designing positional evaluation tables for men and kings, giving progress-based bonuses toward promotion, home-row defensive bonuses, and adjustments for center versus edge columns.

For kings I'm adding a centrality bonus based on distance from the board's center. Then I'm setting up the negamax search with transposition tables, time-check counters, terminal loss scoring when a side has no moves, and move generation with capture detection.

I'm considering skipping depth reduction for forced single moves so captures don't get shortchanged, though I need to watch out for infinite loops with quiet forced moves. I'm sketching out the transposition table lookup keyed by board state and side, storing depth, value, flag, and best move.

Now I'm setting up move ordering: TT best move first, then captures ranked by number captured, then quiet moves scored by advancement toward promotion. For the search itself, I'm doing iterative deepening at the root with a full alpha-beta window, recording the best move each iteration and stopping when the time budget runs out.

Writing king move directions...

Building piece-square tables...

I'm finishing the evaluation function by summing material and positional scores across both sides, then adding a small trade incentive that rewards simplifying the position when ahead in material. Now I'm starting the search function's core loop, beginning with node counting and the depth/alpha-beta termination check.

Adding transposition table logic...

Actually, I need to be careful about extending capture sequences too deeply at low depth, since chaining extensions could blow up the search - I should cap it so a forced capture at depth zero doesn't recurse indefinitely.

Still writing search logic...

Still writing policy function...

For iterative deepening at root, I'll order moves with the previous best first each depth and compute values with search, tracking the best so far. If a timeout hits mid-iteration, I can safely use the current iteration's best move since, with full-window search, any move that beats alpha at this deeper depth is genuinely better than the prior best.

On timeout, the exception skips the score append for that move, so `best` correctly retains the last completed iteration's choice rather than a partial one. I'm also double-checking that the transposition table persists safely across depths within the same search call, and noting that exact TT hits at internal nodes don't propagate the best move upward, which could be worth revisiting.

I want to tighten the timing check to every 256 nodes instead of 1024, since each node likely costs 30-50µs with move generation, giving finer granularity closer to the 0.6s budget. I'm also verifying that the pending-move state comparison uses the exact board tuple, which should be safe enough as a proxy for matching game state.

On the multi-jump edge case, I'm concluding that stopping generation once a piece reaches the last row matches how step-based engines behave, so returning just the first segment of a multi-jump should be fine even if the engine expects full sequences — the risk is acceptable given English rules allow any capture, and multi-jumps are generally too valuable to deprioritize in favor of single jumps.
